'''Eric-Jan Wagenmakers''' (born May 21, 1972) is a Dutch mathematical psychologist. He is a professor at the Methodology Unit in the Department of Psychology at the [[University of Amsterdam]] (UvA).<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ejwagenmakers.com/cvEJ.pdf |title=Eric-Jan Wagenmakers Curriculum Vitae |access-date=2018-05-26}}</ref> Since 2012, he has also been Professor of Neurocognitive Modeling: Interdisciplinary Integration at UvA's Faculty of Social and Behavioral Sciences.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-05-15|url=http://www.uva.nl/en/content/news/professor-appointments/2012/05/dr-e-j-wagenmakers.html |title=Dr E.J. Wagenmakers  |last=Amsterdam |first=Universiteit van |website=www.uva.nl |language=en |access-date=2018-05-27}}</ref> A noted expert on [[research methods]] in psychology, he has been highly critical of some dubious practices by his fellow psychologists, including [[Daryl Bem]]'s research purporting to find support for the [[parapsychological]] concept of [[extrasensory perception]],<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://slate.com/health-and-science/2017/06/daryl-bem-proved-esp-is-real-showed-science-is-broken.html |title=Daryl Bem Proved ESP Is Real. Which Means Science Is Broken. |last=Engber |first=Daniel |date=2017-05-17 |website=Slate Magazine |language=en |access-date=2018-05-27}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/01/06/science/06esp.html |title=Journal's Article on ESP Is Expected to Prompt Outrage |last=Carey |first=Benedict |date=2011 |work=The New York Times |access-date=2018-05-27 |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> and the tendency for psychologists in general to favor the publication of studies with surprising, eye-catching results.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.chronicle.com/article/As-Dutch-Research-Scandal/129746 |title=As Dutch Research Scandal Unfolds, Social Psychologists Question Themselves |last=Shea |first=Christopher |date=2011-11-13 |website=The Chronicle of Higher Education |access-date=2018-05-27}}</ref> He has also been actively addressing the [[replication crisis]] in psychology by helping to conduct a series of studies aimed at reproducing a 1988 study on the supposed effects of smiling on the perceived funniness of [[cartoon]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Replication studies: Bad copy |last=Yong |first=Ed |date=2012-05-16 |journal=Nature |issue=7398 |volume=485 |pages=298–300 |language=en |doi=10.1038/485298a |pmid=22596136 |s2cid=4321991 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2012Natur.485..298Y }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.nature.com/news/psychologists-argue-about-whether-smiling-makes-cartoons-funnier-1.20929 |title=Psychologists argue about whether smiling makes cartoons funnier |last=Skibba |first=Ramin |date=2016-11-03 |journal=Nature |access-date=2018-05-27 |language=en |doi=10.1038/nature.2016.20929 }}</ref> František Bartoš, Dr Wagenmakers, [[Alexandra Sarafoglou]], [[Henrik Godmann]], and many colleagues were awarded the 2024 [[Ig Nobel Prize|Ig Nobel]] Probability Prize for "showing, both in theory and by 350,757 experiments, that when you [[Coin flipping|flip a coin]], it tends to land on the same side as it started."<ref>{{Cite journal |arxiv=2310.04153 |last1=Bartoš |first1=František |last2=Sarafoglou |first2=Alexandra |last3=Godmann
